title: CI/CD Pipelines
tagline: Continuous Integration, Continuous Delivery, and Continuous Deployment — automated pipelines that build, test, and ship software on every commit.

sections.content:
Picture a team of twelve engineers all working on the same codebase. Without discipline, each developer builds a feature in isolation for two weeks, then on 'merge day' everyone tries to combine their changes at once. The result is notorious: conflicting edits, tests that only passed locally, deployment scripts that were never updated, and a weekend of firefighting just to release a feature that should have taken an afternoon. This is **integration hell**, and it plagued software teams throughout the 1990s and 2000s.

**CI/CD** — Continuous Integration, Continuous Delivery, and Continuous Deployment — is the industry's systematic answer to that problem. The core idea is deceptively simple: instead of integrating code rarely and deploying manually, do both constantly and automatically. Every code push triggers a pipeline that builds the software, runs the tests, and (depending on your setup) ships it to production. Problems surface in minutes rather than weeks, when the change is still fresh in the author's mind.

**Continuous Integration (CI)** means every commit is automatically compiled and tested. The word 'continuous' is key: not once a week, not on Fridays before a release — on every single push. CI gives the team a shared reality: if the pipeline is green, the codebase works. If it is red, someone broke it, and their name is on the commit.

**Continuous Delivery (CD)** extends CI by keeping the codebase in an always-deployable state. At any moment, a human can press a button and ship the latest green build to production. **Continuous Deployment** takes this one step further and removes the human button entirely: every passing build is automatically deployed. These three ideas are additive layers, and understanding where each one begins and ends is essential for both interviews and real-world design decisions.

flowchart LR

sections.title: The Automated Airport Baggage Conveyor
sections.content:
Think of a major international airport's baggage system. In the old days, every bag was carried by hand from check-in to the plane — it was slow, inconsistent, and bags got lost or put on the wrong flight constantly. Now imagine an automated conveyor that takes every bag the instant it is tagged and runs it through a sequence of automated checks: weight scan (build check), X-ray (security / linting), routing label verification (type check), and a final inspection gate before it reaches the departure hall (integration tests).

**CI is the conveyor belt.** The moment a developer pushes code (tags a bag), the belt starts moving and checks begin automatically. A bag that fails the X-ray is flagged immediately and pulled out — the developer gets a notification within minutes. A bag that passes all checks is cleared and given a unique tracking number. In CI terms that tracking number is the **artifact**: a versioned, immutable build output (a Docker image, a compiled binary, a release tarball) that is created exactly once and tagged with the git commit SHA.

**Continuous Delivery** means the cleared, tagged bag always arrives at the departure gate ready to board. The gate agent (a human engineer) decides when to actually load it onto the plane. **Continuous Deployment** removes even that final decision: every bag that clears inspection is automatically loaded. The key insight is that once you trust the automated checks completely, there is no reason to pause. The conveyor never stops, every bag is treated identically, and problems are always caught at the scanner — never discovered mid-flight.

sections.title: The Three Tiers: CI vs. Continuous Delivery vs. Continuous Deployment
sections.content:
These three terms are often used interchangeably in casual conversation, which creates real confusion. Here is the precise distinction:

**Continuous Integration** is purely about the development loop. The practice requires that every developer integrates their work into the shared branch frequently — at least daily, ideally on every commit — and that an automated system immediately runs a build and a test suite against the integrated code. The goal is to detect conflicts and regressions as early as possible, while the author can still remember what they changed. Teams practicing CI typically have short-lived feature branches (a few hours to a couple of days) and pull requests that are small enough to review in fifteen minutes.

**Continuous Delivery** adds the deployment dimension but keeps a human in the loop. After CI passes, an automated pipeline prepares the release artifact and can deploy it to staging environments for further testing. Deploying to *production*, however, requires a deliberate human action — clicking 'Approve' or 'Deploy'. The philosophy is that the system is *always ready* to ship; the business decides *when* to ship. This suits products where marketing, legal, or business timing matters: you might want to hold a feature until a product launch date even though it has been technically ready for a week.

**Continuous Deployment** removes the human gate entirely. Every commit that passes all automated checks goes to production automatically, sometimes within minutes of being merged. This sounds alarming but is practiced by companies like Netflix, Amazon, and Etsy, who deploy hundreds of times per day. The key enabler is confidence in the test suite and in fast rollback mechanisms: if a deployment causes an error spike, the system automatically rolls back or the engineer can redeploy the previous artifact in seconds. Continuous Deployment only works when you have mature monitoring and observability in place.

sections.title: Anatomy of a Pipeline: Stage by Stage
sections.content:
A CI/CD pipeline is a directed sequence of stages. Each stage must succeed before the next one begins. Failing fast — stopping the pipeline as soon as one stage fails — is intentional: it saves compute time and gives the developer the clearest possible signal about what broke.

**Stage 1: Source.** The pipeline is triggered by a Git event. Common triggers include: a push to any branch, a pull request opened or updated, a push specifically to `main`, or a scheduled cron job (for nightly integration tests). The CI system checks out the exact commit SHA that triggered the run, ensuring reproducibility.

**Stage 2: Install and Cache.** Dependencies are installed. In Node.js this is `npm ci` — a strict, reproducible install that reads `package-lock.json` exactly and fails if it is out of sync with `package.json`. Dependency installation is cached aggressively: if `package-lock.json` has not changed since the last run, the cached `node_modules` is restored in seconds rather than minutes.

**Stage 3: Build and Lint.** Source code is compiled (TypeScript to JavaScript, Sass to CSS, etc.) and a linter checks for style and potential errors. This stage is fast — under 60 seconds for most projects. Its purpose is to catch syntax errors and obvious mistakes before spending time on tests.

**Stage 4: Unit Tests.** Isolated, fast tests run against individual functions and components with all external dependencies mocked. A good unit test suite should complete in under two minutes. Any single test failure stops the pipeline here. Coverage reports are generated and often uploaded as artifacts for later review.

**Stage 5: Integration Tests.** Tests that exercise real I/O — database queries, HTTP calls to other services — run in this stage. These are slower and may require spinning up a database container (using Docker Compose in CI) or connecting to a dedicated test environment. Integration tests find bugs that unit tests miss because mocks are by definition simplified.

**Stage 6: Package / Artifact Creation.** A successful test stage earns the right to produce an artifact. For a containerised application this means running `docker build` and pushing the resulting image to a container registry (Docker Hub, GitHub Container Registry, AWS ECR). The image is tagged with the git SHA: `my-app:abc1234ef`. This tag is the artifact's immutable identity — the same image, untouched, will be deployed to staging and then production.

**Stage 7: Deploy to Staging.** The artifact is deployed to a staging environment that mirrors production configuration as closely as possible. Smoke tests — a small set of high-level checks that the application is alive and the critical paths work — run automatically. E2E tests using a tool like Playwright or Cypress may run here as well.

**Stage 8: Deploy to Production.** In Continuous Delivery, a GitHub Environment with required reviewers gates this step: no one can deploy without an explicit approval. In Continuous Deployment this step runs automatically. Either way, the *same* artifact that was deployed to staging is what goes to production — never a fresh rebuild from source.

sections.title: GitHub Actions: Workflows, Jobs, and Steps
sections.content:
**GitHub Actions** is the dominant CI/CD platform for open-source projects and many enterprise teams. It is deeply integrated with GitHub: pull request status checks, environment protection rules, and deployment logs all live inside the same UI as your code review.

A **workflow** is a YAML file placed in `.github/workflows/`. GitHub Actions scans this directory and registers each file as a separate workflow. One repository can have multiple workflows for different purposes: `ci.yml` for testing on every push, `release.yml` for tagging and publishing, `nightly.yml` for long-running integration suites.

A workflow file has three main sections:

**`on:`** — triggers. This tells GitHub when to run the workflow. Common values: `push` (with optional `branches` filter), `pull_request`, `workflow_dispatch` (manual trigger via the UI), and `schedule` (cron syntax). You can combine multiple triggers.

**`jobs:`** — a map of named jobs. Each job runs on its own virtual machine (`runs-on: ubuntu-latest` is the most common). Jobs run in parallel by default. Use `needs: [other-job]` to declare a dependency and enforce sequential execution. If a job that another `needs` fails, the dependent job is automatically skipped.

**`steps:`** — a list of sequential actions within a job. A step is either a `run:` block (a shell command) or a `uses:` reference to a community action. Community actions are reusable packages published on the GitHub Marketplace. The most common: `actions/checkout@v4` (clones your repo), `actions/setup-node@v4` (installs Node.js), `actions/cache@v4` (restores and saves caches), and `docker/build-push-action@v5` (builds and pushes Docker images).

**Secrets** are encrypted key-value pairs stored in your repository or organisation settings. They are injected at runtime using the `${{ secrets.MY_SECRET }}` expression syntax. They never appear in logs. Secrets are how you pass API keys, SSH private keys, database URLs, and container registry tokens to your pipeline without committing them to source control.

**Expressions and contexts** are GitHub's templating language. `${{ github.sha }}` gives the exact commit hash. `${{ github.ref }}` gives the branch ref (`refs/heads/main`). `${{ github.actor }}` is the username that triggered the run. You use these to conditionally run steps (e.g., only build a Docker image on `main`) and to embed commit metadata into artifact tags.

sections.label: Example
sections.code:
# .github/workflows/ci-cd.yml
name: CI/CD Pipeline

on:
  push:
    branches: [main, develop]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  # ─── Stage 1: Build and Test ────────────────────────────────
  ci:
    name: Build and Test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout source code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Node.js 20
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '20'
          cache: 'npm'        # automatically caches node_modules by lock file hash

      - name: Install dependencies (strict reproducible install)
        run: npm ci

      - name: Run linter
        run: npm run lint

      - name: Type check
        run: npm run type-check

      - name: Run unit tests with coverage
        run: npm test -- --coverage --ci
        env:
          CI: true            # disables interactive watch mode in Jest

      - name: Upload coverage report artifact
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: coverage-report
          path: coverage/
          retention-days: 7

  # ─── Stage 2: Build Docker Image (main branch only) ─────────
  build-and-push:
    name: Build Docker Image
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: ci                 # will NOT run if ci job fails
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Build and push Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: |
            ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}
            ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest
          # Tag with git SHA = immutable artifact identity
          # 'latest' is a convenience alias for the most recent build

  # ─── Stage 3: Deploy to Production (manual approval gate) ───
  deploy-production:
    name: Deploy to Production
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: build-and-push
    environment: production   # GitHub Environment: requires reviewer approval

    steps:
      - name: Deploy via SSH
        run: |
          ssh -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no deploy@${{ secrets.PROD_HOST }} \
            "docker pull ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }} && \
             docker compose up -d --no-deps app"
        env:
          SSH_PRIVATE_KEY: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_SSH_KEY }}
sections.explanation: This three-job workflow chains via `needs:`. The `ci` job runs on every push and every pull request — it is the fastest feedback loop. `build-and-push` only runs when CI passes AND the push is to `main`, producing a Docker image tagged with the git SHA. `deploy-production` uses a GitHub Environment named 'production' — you configure required reviewers in the repository's Environments settings, turning this into a one-click manual approval gate. This is Continuous Delivery: always ready, human-gated final step.

sections.title: Artifact Immutability and Environment Promotion
sections.content:
One of the most important concepts in CI/CD — and one that many teams get wrong — is **artifact immutability**. The core rule is: build once, promote the same artifact through all environments.

A common anti-pattern is to rebuild from source for each environment: `docker build` on the developer's laptop, then `docker build` again in the staging deployment, then `docker build` again in production. This looks symmetrical but is subtly broken. Build outputs depend on timestamps, installed tool versions, the network (package registry availability), and sometimes environment variables. Two builds from the same source commit can produce different binaries. This means you are never truly testing what you are shipping.

The correct approach: CI produces exactly one artifact (one Docker image) tagged with the git SHA. That image is pushed to a container registry. Staging deployment pulls that image by SHA. After staging tests pass, production deployment pulls the *same* image by *the same* SHA. You are guaranteed that what was tested is what runs in production.

**Semantic versioning** adds a human-readable layer on top of SHA tags. When you decide to cut a release, you add a `v1.4.2` tag to the git commit, and a release pipeline adds that tag to the existing image in the registry. `v1.4.2` points to the same image layers as `abc1234ef` — no rebuild.

**Environment-specific configuration** is handled separately from the artifact. Database URLs, API keys, feature flags, log levels — these are injected at runtime via environment variables or a secrets manager (AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault, Kubernetes secrets). The image itself is environment-agnostic. This separation of code artifact from configuration is known as the **Twelve-Factor App** principle III ("Store config in the environment").

sections.mermaid:
flowchart LR
    A["git commit\nabc1234"]
    A --> B["CI build"]
    B --> C["Image: my-app:abc1234\n(pushed to registry)"]
    C --> D["Staging\ndeploys abc1234"]
    D --> E["Tests pass"]
    E --> F["Production\ndeploys abc1234"]
    F --> G["Same image\ndifferent config"]
sections.caption: Artifact promotion: one image is built from the commit and promoted through environments unchanged. Configuration differs; the code artifact does not.

sections.title: Branch Strategy and Trunk-Based Development
sections.content:
How you use Git branches directly shapes your CI/CD effectiveness. There are two dominant strategies:

**Feature Branch Workflow (GitHub Flow)**: Every piece of work gets its own short-lived branch. When the work is done, a pull request is opened and CI runs against the branch. After review and green CI, the branch is merged into `main`. The `main` branch is always deployable. This is the most common strategy for teams practicing Continuous Delivery.

**Trunk-Based Development**: All developers commit directly to `main` (or to very short-lived branches that live less than a day). Features that are not yet ready for users are hidden behind **feature flags** — runtime toggles that enable or disable code paths without a deployment. This is the strategy used by teams practicing true Continuous Deployment. It forces very small commits and requires strong confidence in the test suite.

Both strategies share the **golden rule**: the default branch (`main` or `trunk`) must always be green. It must always build, always pass tests, and always be deployable. The moment the main branch is broken, every developer in the team is blocked — they cannot confidently rebase their work, they cannot deploy a hotfix, and they cannot trust CI results.

Enforcing this rule requires **branch protection rules** in GitHub: require all status checks to pass before merging, require at least one reviewer approval, and prevent force-pushes to `main`. If a bad commit slips through, the correct response is to immediately revert it — create a revert commit and merge it — rather than piling on fix commits. A quick revert restores the green state and lets everyone continue while the actual fix is developed properly on a branch.

sections.label: Example
sections.code:
# ── Advanced GitHub Actions patterns ──────────────────────────

# PATTERN 1: Matrix builds — test across Node versions in parallel
jobs:
  test-matrix:
    strategy:
      matrix:
        node-version: [18, 20, 22]
        os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest]
      fail-fast: false        # don't cancel other matrix jobs on first failure
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node-version }}
      - run: npm ci && npm test

# PATTERN 2: Caching node_modules manually (more control)
  with-manual-cache:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/cache@v4
        id: npm-cache
        with:
          path: node_modules
          key: npm-${{ runner.os }}-${{ hashFiles('package-lock.json') }}
          restore-keys: npm-${{ runner.os }}-
      - name: Install only when cache misses
        if: steps.npm-cache.outputs.cache-hit != 'true'
        run: npm ci

# PATTERN 3: Run jobs conditionally
  e2e-tests:
    needs: ci
    # Only run E2E on main — too slow and expensive for every PR
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx playwright install --with-deps
      - run: npm run test:e2e

# PATTERN 4: Environment secrets and outputs between jobs
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      image-tag: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.version }}
    steps:
      - id: meta
        run: echo "version=${{ github.sha }}" >> $GITHUB_OUTPUT

  deploy:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "Deploying ${{ needs.build.outputs.image-tag }}"
sections.explanation: Matrix builds fan out a single job definition across combinations of parameters, running all combinations in parallel. This is how you guarantee your library works on Node 18, 20, and 22 without writing three separate job blocks. Conditional execution with `if:` keeps expensive jobs (E2E tests, cross-platform builds) off the hot path of every pull request. The `outputs` pattern lets jobs pass data to downstream jobs without writing to files.

sections.title: Pipeline Performance: Speed is a Feature
sections.content:
A CI pipeline that takes 45 minutes to run is a significant problem, not just an inconvenience. Slow pipelines break the core value proposition: if feedback arrives 45 minutes after a push, the developer has long since switched context, started a new task, and mentally unloaded the code they wrote. Fixing a bug found instantly is ten times faster than fixing one found after a context switch.

Pipeline optimisation falls into a few categories:

**Caching dependencies** is almost always the first win. `npm install` or `pip install` on a cold runner can take 2-4 minutes. With caching, a cache hit (which happens on most runs) restores in 10-20 seconds. The cache key is the hash of the lock file — when dependencies change, the cache misses and a fresh install runs; otherwise the cache is used.

**Parallelising independent jobs** is the second major lever. Lint, type-check, and unit tests are all independent of each other. Instead of running them sequentially in one job (5 min), split them into three parallel jobs (2 min total, since the longest determines wall time). GitHub Actions runs parallel jobs on separate VMs simultaneously at no extra wall-clock cost.

**Separating test tiers** keeps pull request feedback fast. Unit tests run on every PR (they must — that is CI). Integration tests and E2E tests can be gated to the `main` branch only, or run as a separate nightly job. The tradeoff is that PRs get slightly less coverage, but the fast feedback on the common case is usually worth it.

**Fail fast** means putting the cheapest, most likely-to-fail checks first. Run the linter before the test suite — a lint failure costs 30 seconds instead of 10 minutes.

**Self-hosted runners** are an option for high-volume teams who find GitHub-hosted runners too slow or too expensive. You run the runner software on your own infrastructure (a powerful EC2 instance, a local server) and configure it with more CPU, RAM, and local caches. The tradeoff is operational overhead of managing the runner fleet.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart LR
    A["Push to PR"]
    A --> B["Job: Lint\n30s"]
    A --> C["Job: Type-check\n60s"]
    A --> D["Job: Unit tests\n90s"]
    B --> E{"All pass?"}
    C --> E
    D --> E
    E -- "Yes" --> F["PR ready\nfor review"]
    E -- "No" --> G["Notify and\nblock merge"]

sections.title: Secrets Management and Security in Pipelines
sections.content:
CI/CD pipelines are high-value attack targets. A compromised pipeline can push malicious code to production, exfiltrate credentials, or poison the artifact registry. Security is not optional.

**Never commit secrets to source control.** This is the most important rule. API keys, database connection strings, SSH private keys, container registry tokens — none of these belong in `.github/workflows/` files, in `.env` files that are checked in, or anywhere else in the repository. GitHub Secrets stores them encrypted at rest, and they are only decrypted and injected into the runner's environment at runtime. They never appear in logs (GitHub Actions automatically masks any string that matches a registered secret).

**Principle of least privilege**: each job should have only the permissions it actually needs. GitHub Actions workflows have a default `GITHUB_TOKEN` with read/write access to the repository. For most jobs that do not need to push images or create releases, restrict this to read-only with `permissions: read-all` at the top of the workflow. For the specific job that pushes a Docker image, grant `packages: write` only on that job.

**Pinning action versions**: `uses: actions/checkout@v4` is a mutable reference — GitHub can update what `v4` points to. If a malicious actor compromises the `actions/checkout` package and tags a new version as `v4`, your workflow would execute their code. Pinning to an immutable commit SHA — `uses: actions/checkout@11bd71901bbe5b1630ceea73d27597364c9af683` — prevents this supply-chain attack. It is verbose but much safer for production pipelines.

**OIDC (OpenID Connect) for cloud credentials**: Instead of storing long-lived cloud provider secrets (AWS access keys, GCP service account keys) in GitHub Secrets, modern pipelines use OIDC. The CI runner requests a short-lived token from the cloud provider, authenticated by GitHub's OIDC identity provider. The token expires after the job completes. This eliminates the risk of a stolen secret being used outside the pipeline.

**Branch protection on secrets**: GitHub allows you to restrict which branches can access environment secrets. Only `main` should be able to access production credentials. Pull request branches from forks should never have access to any production secrets.

sections.title: Rolling Back: The Other Half of Deployment
sections.content:
Fast deployment is only valuable if fast rollback is equally easy. No matter how good your test suite is, bugs reach production — edge cases, load-related issues, data-specific bugs that were never tested. The goal is not zero production incidents; it is minimising their duration.

With immutable artifacts tagged by git SHA, rollback is straightforward: redeploy the previous artifact. If `v1.4.3` has a bug, you pull and run `v1.4.2` — the same Docker image that ran successfully in production before the last deployment. This takes seconds.

**Blue/green deployments** maintain two identical production environments (blue = current, green = new). Traffic is routed to blue while the new version is deployed to green. Smoke tests run against green. If they pass, a load balancer switch flips traffic to green in an instant. If anything goes wrong, the switch flips back. Blue and green then swap roles for the next deployment.

**Canary deployments** are a more gradual approach: the new version is deployed to a small subset of production servers (say, 5% of traffic) while the old version handles the rest. Metrics (error rate, latency, business KPIs) are monitored. If the canary looks healthy, the percentage is gradually increased. If problems appear, the canary is removed and all traffic returns to the old version. Canary deployments are how large companies like Netflix and Google ship code to billions of users safely.

**Feature flags** decouple deployment from feature release. Code can be deployed to production while the feature is disabled for all users. Once the team is ready, the flag is flipped — no deployment required. If the feature causes problems, the flag is flipped back — again, no deployment. This is the ultimate low-risk release mechanism, and it is why trunk-based development and Continuous Deployment work at scale.

**Historical context:** The term 'Continuous Integration' was coined by Grady Booch in 1991 but was popularised by Kent Beck as part of Extreme Programming (XP) in the late 1990s. The first widely adopted CI server was **CruiseControl**, released in 2001 by ThoughtWorks. **Hudson** (later forked as **Jenkins**) emerged in 2004 and became the industry standard for the next decade. Travis CI (2011) introduced the idea of CI-as-a-service with YAML configuration files in the repository — a design that directly influenced every modern platform including GitHub Actions (2018), GitLab CI, and CircleCI.

**Common mistakes and interview traps:**

**Treating CI as optional on small projects.** CI is cheapest to set up on day one when the codebase is tiny. Retrofitting it onto a large legacy project is expensive. Start with CI from the first commit.

**Rebuilding the artifact per environment.** Build once, promote everywhere. If your staging and production builds are separate `docker build` commands, you are not testing what you deploy.

**Long-lived feature branches.** A branch that lives for two weeks accumulates a massive integration delta. Merge small, merge often, use feature flags to hide unfinished work.

**Testing everything in the PR pipeline.** Slow E2E tests that run on every PR undermine fast feedback. Move them to the post-merge pipeline on `main`.

**Hard-coding environment config in the image.** The image should contain only code. Config comes from environment variables or a secrets manager at runtime — this is what makes the same image deployable to staging and production.

items: **CI (Continuous Integration)** automatically builds and tests every commit within minutes, catching integration bugs while the author still has context — eliminating 'integration hell' from large team codebases.

**Continuous Delivery** keeps `main` always deployable with a human-gated production push; **Continuous Deployment** removes that gate — every green build ships automatically, requiring mature monitoring and fast rollback.

**Pipeline stages** (install → lint → build → unit test → integration test → package → staging → production) are sequential quality gates: failing fast at the earliest possible stage saves time and gives the clearest signal.

**Artifact immutability** is the cornerstone of reliable deployments: build the Docker image or binary exactly once, tag it with the git SHA, and promote the same artifact through staging and production — never rebuild from source per environment.

**GitHub Actions** workflows in `.github/workflows/` define jobs that run on virtual machines; `needs:` chains them, parallel jobs cut wall time, and `if:` conditions restrict expensive stages to `main` only.
**Secrets** belong in encrypted secret stores (GitHub Secrets, Vault, AWS Secrets Manager), never in YAML files. OIDC short-lived tokens are the modern best practice for cloud provider access.

**Rollback is as important as deployment**: immutable artifacts enable instant rollback by redeploying the previous SHA; blue/green and canary strategies allow zero-downtime rollouts with fast recovery on failure.

quiz.question: What is the precise difference between Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment?
options: Continuous Delivery runs tests automatically; Continuous Deployment skips the test stage for speed.
Continuous Delivery keeps the codebase deployable with a human approval gate before production; Continuous Deployment deploys automatically on every green build.
Continuous Deployment requires a container orchestrator like Kubernetes; Continuous Delivery works with any infrastructure.
Continuous Delivery skips staging environments to ship faster to users.
quiz.explanation: Continuous Delivery means every green build is ready to ship, but a human decides when to push the button. Continuous Deployment removes that human gate entirely — every passing build automatically reaches production. Both require the same CI foundation.

quiz.question: Why should a Docker image be tagged with the git commit SHA rather than a generic tag like 'latest'?
options: SHA tags reduce the Docker image layer count and make images smaller.
The 'latest' tag is reserved for public Docker Hub images only.
The SHA tag creates an immutable link between the running artifact and the exact source commit it was built from, enabling reliable rollbacks.
SHA tags allow Docker to skip rebuilding unchanged layers in CI.
quiz.explanation: Tagging with the git SHA makes artifacts immutable and fully traceable. You can always determine which code version runs in production. Rolling back means redeploying the previous SHA image — the same binary that ran before the problematic deployment, with no rebuild needed.

quiz.question: In GitHub Actions, what does `needs: ci` on a job accomplish?
options: The job will run in the same virtual machine as the `ci` job, sharing its file system.
The job will only start after the `ci` job completes successfully; if `ci` fails, this job is skipped.
The job will download all artifacts produced by the `ci` job automatically.
The job requires Node.js CI mode (`CI=true` environment variable) to be set.
quiz.explanation: `needs:` declares a dependency between jobs. A job with `needs: ci` waits for the `ci` job to finish successfully before it starts. If `ci` fails, all dependent jobs are skipped — preventing a broken build from reaching deploy stages.

quiz.question: What is the key advantage of `npm ci` over `npm install` in a CI pipeline?
options: It installs only production dependencies, making the image smaller.
It performs a clean install strictly from `package-lock.json` and fails if the lock file is out of sync, guaranteeing reproducible builds.
It automatically upgrades packages to the latest compatible semver versions.
It skips post-install scripts to prevent arbitrary code execution in CI.
quiz.explanation: `npm ci` deletes `node_modules` first, then installs exactly the versions listed in `package-lock.json`. It fails immediately if `package.json` and the lock file disagree. This guarantees that every CI run uses an identical dependency tree, eliminating the 'works on my machine' class of bugs.

quiz.question: Which best describes the principle of 'build once, promote the same artifact'?
options: Run `docker build` on every server in the production fleet to ensure each server has a fresh image.
Create a separate CI pipeline for staging and another for production, each building from the same source.
Build the artifact (Docker image or binary) exactly once in CI, tag it immutably, and deploy that same artifact to staging and then production without rebuilding.
Use a monorepo build tool to compile all services in a single command.
quiz.explanation: Building once and promoting the same artifact guarantees that what was tested in staging is exactly what runs in production. Rebuilding per environment introduces the risk that two builds from the same source commit produce different outputs due to tool versions, timestamps, or network availability.

quiz.question: A team's CI pipeline takes 40 minutes to run on every pull request, slowing developer iteration significantly. What is the most effective first optimisation?
options: Switch from GitHub Actions to a self-hosted runner cluster.
Remove E2E tests from the pipeline entirely.
Cache dependencies between runs and split lint, type-check, and unit tests into parallel jobs.
Reduce the number of unit tests to only the most critical paths.
quiz.explanation: Caching eliminates repeated dependency installation (often 2-4 minutes per run). Parallelising independent jobs (lint, type-check, unit tests) means wall time equals the slowest job rather than their sum. These two changes together often cut pipeline time by 50-70% without sacrificing quality gates.

quiz.question: What does it mean for the `main` branch to be 'always green'?
options: The branch has a green status badge displayed in the GitHub UI.
Only engineers with 'green' clearance level can push to the branch.
Every commit on `main` has passed all automated tests; the codebase is always in a deployable state.
The branch automatically deploys to production after each merge completes.
quiz.explanation: An always-green `main` means CI has verified that every commit on the default branch builds and passes all tests. Branch protection rules enforce this by requiring status checks to pass before a PR can merge. A green `main` means you can deploy at any moment with confidence.

quiz.question: Why should CI/CD pipeline secrets (API keys, credentials) be stored in GitHub Secrets rather than in the workflow YAML file?
options: YAML files cannot contain strings longer than 128 characters, so secrets would be truncated.
Workflow YAML files are committed to the repository and visible to anyone with read access; GitHub Secrets are encrypted and only injected at runtime.
GitHub Actions cannot read environment variables defined in YAML files directly.
Secrets in YAML cause pipeline timeouts on repositories with more than 100 contributors.
quiz.explanation: Workflow files live in the repository and are readable by all contributors (and publicly by default for open-source repos). Hard-coded credentials would be immediately visible. GitHub Secrets stores values encrypted, masks them in all log output, and injects them only into the runner's environment at execution time.

quiz.question: What is a matrix build strategy in GitHub Actions used for?
options: Deploying to multiple production regions simultaneously with load balancing.
Running the same job across multiple combinations of parameters (e.g., Node versions, operating systems) in parallel.
Splitting a large test suite into shards that run on separate runners.
Building both a debug and production version of a Docker image in one job.
quiz.explanation: Matrix builds fan out a single job definition across a set of parameter combinations. For example, `node-version: [18, 20, 22]` creates three parallel jobs, each running on a different Node version. This is how you guarantee cross-version compatibility without writing separate job blocks.

quiz.question: A blue/green deployment strategy primarily achieves which of the following?
options: It reduces Docker image size by splitting the application into blue (frontend) and green (backend) layers.
It allows zero-downtime deployments with instant rollback by maintaining two identical environments and switching traffic between them.
It enforces that blue commits are deployed on weekdays and green commits on weekends.
It runs the new version on 5% of traffic and gradually increases the percentage over time.
quiz.explanation: Blue/green keeps two production environments. The new version is deployed to the idle environment, smoke-tested, and then a load balancer instantly switches all traffic to it. If problems appear, the switch flips back in seconds — true zero-downtime with instant rollback. Gradually increasing traffic percentage describes a canary deployment, which is a different strategy.
